title: The Nervous System Triangle
summary: The polyvagal-informed model behind everything we teach: survival mode versus rest-and-digest.

sourceNote: Understanding the Triangle guide
title: How Clients Get Here
summary: Tipping points, and how we talk about personality without assigning blame.
body:
Most clients can identify a tipping point: a traumatic event, a virus such as COVID, or a series of stressful events compounding in a short period.

### Key message for clients
A client's personality did not cause their illness. Predisposed traits don't create a hypersensitive nervous system, but they raise the chance of developing one when a tipping-point event occurs, and certain traits may be keeping the illness going.

This distinction lets coaches work on the patterns that maintain illness without implying that the client is to blame for having it.

sourceNote: Understanding the Triangle guide
title: The Triangle and the Capacity Line
summary: The six bands of the triangle, from Green through to Red, and what each looks like.
body:
Picture the nervous system as an upside-down triangle. At the top sits the **capacity line**: the ability to sustain everyday activity at a high level. Moving down the triangle, the line gets shorter, meaning less capacity. Each zone is identified by color.

### Green
Where healthy people spend most of their time. Happy, healthy, confident, with a very resilient nervous system. Clear thinking; energy feels accessible; confidence; social connection feels natural.

### Upper Yellow
The normal stress response. When something bothers us, we dip here briefly and return to Green. Everyone experiences this. Irritability; moodiness; feeling annoyed; slight tension.

### Mid Yellow
Stress compounds and isn't addressed in a healthy way. Irritability turns to anger and anxiety appears. Anger; frustration; mild anxiety; slight panic symptoms.

### Lower Yellow
Approaching overwhelm. Emotional regulation becomes difficult, sleep issues emerge, and hormonal imbalances can start.

### Orange
The highest point on the wall before the fall. The nervous system is at its limit and saying "enough is enough." Panic attacks, gut issues, no energy, absolute exhaustion.

### Red (Freeze)
The nervous system has shut down to protect the person, like a possum playing dead. An involuntary survival response, not laziness or failure. Completely debilitated; sensitive to light and sound; deep depression.

Note: the Yellow bands above describe the triangle as taught to clients. The Low, Mid, and High Yellow recovery phases in the zone guides use different descriptions.

sourceNote: Understanding the Triangle guide
title: Why Clients Have Their Specific Symptoms
summary: Symptoms tend to land on whatever the client valued most before illness.
body:
The things a client valued most before getting sick often become their biggest struggles during illness. When the brain flips into freeze mode, it dims whatever was most "lit up" in their healthy life. Exploring this connection helps clients make sense of their particular symptoms.

**Miguel.** Before: loved food, trying new restaurants, walking Disney parks, shopping. During: energy issues, gut problems, food intolerances, difficulty walking.

**Coach Crista.** Before: prided herself on studying, remembering information, and digesting complex material. During: brain fog; inability to focus and concentrate.

sourceNote: Understanding the Triangle guide
title: Climbing the Triangle: The Recovery Sequence
summary: Six steps from freeze to high capacity, and the approach that belongs to each.
body:
Different zones require different approaches, and using the wrong approach at the wrong time can hurt rather than help. Matching the approach to the zone is the single most important principle for consistent coaching.

### 1. Getting out of freeze — Red — Deep restorative rest
Rest of the body and of the mind: limit worry, concern, fear, and anxiousness. Returning energy hits the nervous system first; it won't arrive as "feeling better."

### 2. Wired and tired — Orange — Detachment from experience
As energy returns, clients feel wired, overwhelmed, and exhausted, and may cry for no reason or swing between anger, sadness, and anxiety. These feelings are inevitable at this stage; don't panic about them.

### 3. Constant symptoms — Lower Yellow — Adjustment period cycles
Symptoms settle to a constant 6–7/10. Introduce gentle adjustment periods: stretch the nervous system like a rubber band, then allow recovery.

### 4. Stabilization — Build the foundation
Capacity may not rise for many adjustment periods, but the client is becoming more stable: responding better to symptoms, not panicking as quickly, feeling calmer. Stability comes before capacity.

### 5. Capacity building — Yellow to Green — Gradual expansion
Physical progress becomes noticeable: walking farther, doing more without flares. Don't underestimate how long this phase takes.

### 6. High capacity — Upper Yellow / Green — Reverse the approach
Stop paying so much attention to levels, allow gentle pushing, trust intuition, and relearn how to be normal. Unlearn careful pacing and reintegrate into the world.

sourceNote: Understanding the Triangle guide
title: The Boat Analogy and the Adjustment Period Cycle
summary: Stretching moves recovery forward; mindset keeps it afloat.
body:
We describe recovery as a boat:

- **Moving forward.** Every gentle stretch of the nervous system (an adjustment period) pushes the boat forward.
- **Staying afloat.** Mindset keeps the boat floating. Without the right mindset, the boat can't move forward.

Each adjustment period follows the same cycle:

1. Gently go out of the comfort zone
2. Flare-up (expected)
3. Rest physically and mentally
4. Flare dies down
5. Repeat

If the client paces appropriately, the flares will be gentle too.

sourceNote: Understanding the Triangle guide
title: Guiding Principles
summary: The nine principles every zone guide and topic module should be consistent with.
body:
> "Recovery does not come from forcing the nervous system into safety — it comes from teaching the nervous system that safety is available again."

We are not teaching clients to eliminate stress, which is neither sustainable nor realistic. We are teaching them to respond to stress differently than they did before.

- Different zones require different approaches; the wrong approach at the wrong time can hurt. (2.5)
- Stability comes before capacity. (2.5)
- Regulation comes before expansion. (Orange)
- Meet clients where they are. (Orange)
- Flare-ups are an expected part of the adjustment cycle, not a failure. (2.5, 2.6, M-03)
- Avoid swinging between over-pushing and over-resting. (Low Yellow, M-04)
- Rest means rest of the mind as well as the body. (2.5, Red)
- Mindset keeps recovery afloat. (2.6)
- Celebrate small wins and progress. (Orange, Green)

sourceNote: Zone pages
title: Zones at a Glance
summary: Side-by-side comparison of all six zones: symptom level, focus, move-up cue, and what to watch for.
body:
### Red
Typical symptoms: constant 10/10. Focus: calm the mind; deep physical rest. Ready to move up when symptoms ease to about 7–9/10, or the client reports more activation, energy, adrenaline, or a wired feeling. Watch for: content that increases fear or stimulation.

### Orange
Typical symptoms: not specified (R-04). Focus: detach from experiences; release activation safely; calm the system. Ready to move up when the client stabilizes and can handle more activity or mindset work. Watch for: pushing too hard (regression to Red) or too little (stagnation).

### Low Yellow
Typical symptoms: constant 6–7/10. Focus: start expanding activity with small, logical steps. Move-up cue not specified (R-06). Watch for: swinging from over-pushing to over-resting.

### Mid Yellow
Typical symptoms: fluctuating; good and bad days. Focus: consistent expansion; fear-free flare response; social and work reintegration. Move-up cue not specified (R-06). Watch for: fear of regression; impatience.

### High Yellow
Typical symptoms: constant mild 1–4/10. Focus: say yes to life; pull back when overwhelmed; gratitude. Move-up cue not specified (R-06). Watch for: catastrophizing or fixating on incomplete recovery.

### Green
Typical symptoms: minimal. Focus: consolidate gains; plan ahead; prevent relapse; celebrate. Relapse signs not specified (R-07).

sourceNote: Red Zone page
title: Red Zone: Freeze, Crash, Shutdown
summary: The toughest phase. Trust has to be built before anything else lands.
body:
### Overview
The client's nervous system is in shutdown or freeze mode, causing extreme physical debilitation and mental shutdown. Symptoms are at their peak and daily life is at its most challenging. The severity at this stage directly parallels how black-and-white or extreme the client's specific imbalances are.

### Recognizing the zone
- Extreme physical debilitation; can barely walk, talk, or eat
- Sensitivity to light and sound
- Deep depression and mental shutdown
- Feeling overwhelmed, anxious, and on edge (see R-01)
- Symptoms at a constant 10/10

### Core coaching message
This stage is temporary and challenging, but recovery is possible. Coaches, including Miguel and the team, have recovered from this exact point, and the client can and will recover by following the same path. Focus on calming the mind and allowing physical rest.

### Immediate priorities
1. Calm the mind. Limit worry, concern, fear, and anxiousness.
2. Provide deep physical rest.

### Practical interventions
- Open a window for fresh air and natural sunlight, if tolerable.
- Play calming nature sounds, such as flowing water or birdsong, if capacity allows.

### Content exposure — strict filtering
Recommended: wins in the main feed, filtered to show only wins (a caregiver can help set this up); the wins portion of call replays, stopping when the call shifts to questions; if capacity is low, chunk replays into 5-minute segments.

Do not expose to: questions in the main feed; full video modules; nervous system education (introduce later, when the client is ready).

### Coach's approach
- **Understand how clients reach Red.** A trigger rarely takes someone all the way to Red; most of the time the lowest a trigger pulls someone is Orange. It is usually extreme behaviors, emotions, personality traits, or mental habits that pull them the extra notch down.
- **Expect protectiveness and mistrust.** The nervous system is extremely protective and very resistant to change. Out of fear, the client will not trust you at first.
- **Build a bridge of trust before anything else.** Clients here are highly limbic and emotional, so the brain needs a counterbalance of calm, logic, and reassurance — enough science that the client feels understood, general enough not to confuse them.
- **Treat recovery as a team effort.** The client also needs to meet you halfway and be willing to take your guidance.
- **Persist with willing clients; escalate persistent resistance.** If a client constantly argues, refuses to listen, and shows ongoing doubt over months, raise it with the coaching team (see R-09).

### Transition cues
- Symptoms are no longer a constant 10/10 and have eased to around 7–9/10: begin moving into Orange Zone guidance.
- The client reports increased activation, energy, adrenaline, or a wired feeling: move to Orange.

### Case study: Laura
Laura had a severe case of COVID. Once the infection had passed, she could barely walk around her house and couldn't sit up for more than 15 minutes at a time. Terrified, she watched a CFS documentary showing a young woman on a feeding tube, unable to speak or move.

Horrified, Laura became afraid of movement itself and pulled back her activity dramatically. Over time she pulled back so far that she is now in the Red Zone herself, and every attempt to move triggers an extreme flare. By treating movement as terrifying, she has signaled to her nervous system that it is dangerous, which continues the loop.

Coaching insight: Laura's extreme, black-and-white behavior is a practice of highly imbalanced levels of fear.

sourceNote: Orange Zone page
title: Orange Zone: High Activation, Wired Recovery
summary: Wired and tired. Regulation comes before expansion.
body:
### Overview
The client is transitioning out of shutdown into high activation and wired energy. This is still debilitating, but it signals real progress from Red. Orange is a phase of heightened awareness in which the client is acutely tuned in to bodily signals. It is transitional: clients who respond well progress to Yellow, and clients who respond poorly can regress to Red.

### Recognizing the zone
- Extreme depression has mostly lifted, replaced by a hyper-emotional state
- Anxiousness paired with exhaustion ("wired and tired")
- Random mood swings: crying for no reason, sudden anger, sadness, or anxiety
- May appear functional while working from a depleted, highly activated state

### Core coaching message
This stage is uncomfortable and challenging, but temporary. Coaches have recovered from it, and with persistence it will end. Focus on not personalizing experiences and allowing them to pass.

### Immediate priorities
1. Detach from experiences.
2. Release activation energy safely.
3. Calm the system after release.

### Practical interventions
- **For emotions:** observe without identifying. "I'm experiencing sadness" rather than "I am sad." Allow emotions to run their course.
- **For physical activation:** briefly shake off adrenaline surges to release the energy, then shift to rest and calming techniques.

### Content exposure
Recommended, in order: Academy Classroom Resources starting with the Thriver Foundations Masterclass; Thriver Mentality video modules for mindset; Symptom Solutions; full Fundamentals A calls including wins and questions. If overwhelmed during a call, leave and watch the replay later.

Do not expose to: overwhelming amounts of content at once; pushing through when feeling overstimulated. (The strict-filtering label conflicts with these recommendations — see R-05.)

### Coach's approach
- Meet clients where they are: they may appear functional but are working from a depleted state.
- Focus on regulation before expansion.
- Teach detachment language.
- Help them recognize sympathetic activation patterns and allow experiences to pass.
- Celebrate small wins; moving out of Red is significant.
- Guide pacing: not so hard they regress to Red, not so little they stagnate.

### Transition cues
- The client stabilizes and can handle more activity or mindset work: move to Yellow Zone guidance.
- Regression risk: pushing too hard can return the client to Red.

sourceNote: Yellow Zone overview page
title: Yellow Zone: Functional Recovery
summary: The longest zone, tiered into Low, Mid, and High. Mostly about conquering fear of expanding.
body:
### Overview
Yellow is a sign of significant progress. The client is moving closer to a balanced state but isn't there yet. It is a phase of cautious optimism in which clients begin to reclaim parts of their lives.

Yellow is by far the longest zone, lasting anywhere from a few weeks to years depending on the individual and their commitment to recovery principles. This stage is far more about **conquering fear related to expanding activity**: going back into the world again and again until the nervous system is conditioned to feel safe.

### The three tiers
- **Low Yellow — Initial Stabilization.** High, constant symptoms that don't respond to rest. The starting line for expanding activity.
- **Mid Yellow — Active Recovery.** Good days and bad days. Doing more, still flaring regularly.
- **High Yellow — Ongoing Recovery.** High functioning with constant mild symptoms. Close to full recovery.

### Coach's approach (all Yellow tiers)
- This is the longest zone. It requires patience and consistent effort over weeks to years.
- Focus on conquering fear related to expanding activity.
- Help the client go back into the world again and again until the nervous system feels safe.
- Encourage more active participation in recovery work.
- Challenge limiting beliefs gently but consistently.
- Support gradual expansion of activities.
- Build confidence in the client's ability to handle setbacks.

sourceNote: Low Yellow tier page
title: Low Yellow: Initial Stabilization
summary: Rest alone won't advance recovery here. This is the starting line for expansion.
body:
### Overview
Symptoms remain noticeably uncomfortable and constant, regardless of rest or gentle activity — a constant 6–7/10.

### Recognizing the zone
**Physical:** high, persistent symptoms that do not significantly improve with rest; no meaningful change whether resting or slightly increasing activity.

**Mental and emotional:** frustration from lack of progress; fear or hesitation to expand activity because of past over-pushing; realization that waiting for symptoms to drop may take too long.

### Core coaching message
Rest alone won't advance recovery here. This is the starting line, even with high symptoms. Avoid swinging from over-pushing to over-resting; gradual, consistent expansion builds capacity.

### Immediate priorities
1. Recognize this as the point to start expanding activity.
2. Overcome fear by introducing small, logical next steps.
3. Prepare for flare-ups as part of the adjustment period process.

### Practical interventions
- Mostly resting on the couch: start moving around the house more consistently.
- Already moving indoors: add short outdoor walks of 1–5 minutes.
- Handling short walks: increase to 5–10 minutes; introduce brief car rides.
- At any level: add a little more to current activity; expect temporary flare-ups and dips.

### Gaps
No content exposure guidance for this tier (R-08). No criteria for moving to Mid Yellow or recognizing regression (R-06).

sourceNote: Mid Yellow tier page
title: Mid Yellow: Active Recovery
summary: Good days and bad days. Keep stacking adjustment periods and start reintegrating.
body:
### Overview
The client shows consistent improvement, with good days and bad days. They can do more but still experience regular symptom flares.

### Recognizing the zone
**Physical:** symptoms fluctuate; can handle moderate activity with planned rest; sleep continuing to improve; primary symptoms still present but more manageable.

**Mental and emotional:** growing confidence mixed with occasional fear of regression; impatience to return to normal life; better emotional regulation than Orange or Low Yellow.

### Core coaching message
You're in the active building phase. Consistency is key: keep stacking good days while managing flares appropriately. Every adjustment period makes your nervous system more resilient.

### Immediate priorities
1. Maintain consistent activity expansion.
2. Build a robust response to flare-ups, without fear.
3. Start reintegrating social and work activities.

### Practical interventions
- Regular walks of 10–20 minutes
- Short social outings, such as coffee with friends or quick errands
- Light household responsibilities
- Part-time or flexible work options, if ready
- Continue stacking adjustment periods

### Gaps
No content exposure guidance (R-08). No criteria for moving to High Yellow or recognizing regression (R-06).

sourceNote: High Yellow tier page
title: High Yellow: Ongoing Recovery
summary: High functioning with mild constant symptoms. Lean into life; shift frustration to gratitude.
body:
### Overview
The client is high functioning and able to live a decent life, but mild underlying symptoms persist.

### Recognizing the zone
**Physical:** capacity for part-time work; can walk 30–40 minutes uninterrupted without flare-ups; can socialize and attend events; constant mild symptoms (1–4/10) make daily life a subtle struggle, though not visible to others.

**Mental and emotional:** frustration from being close to full recovery but not quite there; occasional symptom-free days heighten awareness of lingering issues; tendency to catastrophize or fixate on incomplete recovery.

### Core coaching message
Congratulations on high functioning; this is real progress. Lean into life while listening to your body. Shift focus from frustration to gratitude for your current capacity.

### Immediate priorities
1. Embrace activities to build resilience.
2. Balance participation with pullbacks when overwhelmed.
3. Reframe mindset toward gratitude and living fully.

### Practical interventions
- Say yes to invitations: events, extra work hours, short vacations, plane trips.
- If overwhelmed during an activity, pull back immediately.
- Focus on what the client can do, and practice gratitude to reduce frustration.

Step 6 of the recovery sequence (reverse the approach) begins to apply from Upper Yellow. See 2.5 and R-07.

sourceNote: Green Zone page
title: Green Zone: Recovery State
summary: Minimal symptoms and good capacity. Consolidate, plan ahead, prevent relapse, celebrate.
body:
### Overview
Symptoms are minimal, the nervous system is regulated, and the client has good capacity. This is where integration and expansion happen.

Clients in Green spend more time in a ventral vagal state of safety and connection, characterized by clear thinking, emotional flexibility, and accessible energy.

### Recognizing the zone
- Clear thinking
- Energy feels accessible
- Confidence and emotional flexibility
- Social connection feels natural

### Immediate priorities
1. Consolidate gains.
2. Plan for the future.
3. Prevent relapse.
4. Celebrate progress.

### Practical interventions
Recovery sequence step 6 applies here: stop paying so much attention to levels, allow gentle pushing, trust intuition, relearn how to be normal, and reintegrate into the world.

### Coach's approach
- Support continued growth and expansion.
- Help the client process their recovery journey.
- Prepare the client for independent maintenance of their health.
- Celebrate their success and transformation.

### Gaps
No core coaching message, specific interventions, content guidance, or relapse warning signs yet (R-07). Module M-14 now offers material that could fill these.

sourceNote: 551 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Explaining the Nervous System
summary: Symptoms are the nervous system's protective signals, not evidence of damage.
body:
### Core principle
Symptoms are the nervous system's protective signals, not evidence of damage. Clients recover by giving it repeated, consistent experiences of safety, so our explanations should make symptoms understandable without making them frightening.

### What we do

- **Explain symptoms as protection.** The nervous system is trying to keep the client safe; it perceives danger and responds with symptoms. Crista describes it as a scared, hypervigilant best friend who can only communicate through symptoms.
- **Explain adrenaline and delayed flares.** Junior's two-tank model: Tank A is genuine energy, Tank B is adrenaline. When Tank A runs dry the body switches to Tank B invisibly, the client feels fine, and the bill arrives 24–48 hours later. Jon compares running on adrenaline to using a credit card.
- **Explain total load, not just activity.** Work stress, family pressure, perfectionism, and emotional events all fill the same bucket. A workout that precedes an adjustment period is often just the last scoop in an already full bucket (Crista).
- **Point to evidence that it's the nervous system.** Symptoms that switch or rotate within a day suggest nervous system involvement rather than structural damage (Jon, Ariel).
- **Teach that safety needs repetition.** Sporadic effort doesn't teach the nervous system anything; consistent, frequent experiences do (Jon). Nicole frames this as showing the nervous system the new version of you, not the old one.
- **Explain why hypervigilance undermines progress.** If a client expands successfully but monitors their body the whole time, the brain credits the monitoring for the good outcome rather than learning the activity is safe (Junior).
- **Explain place associations.** Symptoms can ramp up on returning home because the nervous system associates home with being sick (Crista).
- **Offer both routes into the nervous system.** Top-down work uses the mind (reframing, beliefs); bottom-up work uses the body (breathing, posture, pacing, movement). Most clients need both (Junior).

### What we say
- “Adrenaline is a mask.” (Junior)
- “All the pressure we're putting on ourself is pressure we're putting on our nervous system.” (Crista)
- “If you're sporadic with it, the nervous system never learns that it's safe.” (Jon)
- Mini flare-ups are like a car's reversing sensor beeping near a wall: information that you're near your limits, not an emergency (Jon).
- If the nervous system releases capacity and you immediately push it to the limit, it won't trust you with more (Jon).

### What we avoid
- Overly medical or scientific explanations that make recovery sound like an enormous amount of work, especially for exhausted clients (Junior).
- Explanations that imply the client caused their illness (see Part 2.2).
- Analyzing every possible cause of a symptom; this feeds the search for danger.

### Named tools
- **Tank A / Tank B** — Genuine energy versus adrenaline; explains delayed flares and why feeling fine during an activity isn't the whole picture. (Junior)
- **Stress bucket** — All stressors fill one bucket; the final activity isn't the sole cause of an adjustment period. (Crista)
- **Credit card energy** — Adrenaline is borrowed energy that gets paid back the next day. (Jon)
- **Reversing sensor** — Small flares are proximity beeps near the edge of capacity. (Jon)
- **Top-down / bottom-up** — Two complementary routes: mind-based and body-based regulation. (Junior)

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · May 2026 · Crista* — A client blamed a gym session for triggering an adjustment period. Crista walked through everything else in the bucket that month (family crises, travel, emotional processing) so the client wouldn't start avoiding exercise.
- *Integration call · Jan 2026 · Junior* — Junior used the two-tank model to explain post-exertional malaise, then introduced voluntary breaks every 20 minutes so the body never needs to switch to emergency fuel.

sourceNote: 112 call entries; most from Jon, Junior, Ariel
title: Language and Self-Talk
summary: The words clients use about symptoms and themselves are heard by the nervous system as information about danger.
body:
### Core principle
The words clients use about symptoms and themselves are heard by the nervous system as information about danger. We teach neutral, accurate language, and self-talk the client can actually believe.

### What we do

- **Correct dramatic language early and gently.** Replace threat words with neutral descriptions (see the language guide below).
- **Keep phrases believable.** The nervous system has a built-in “BS detector”: saying “I love these symptoms” while hating them doesn't land (Crista). The energy behind the words matters more than the words (Junior).
- **Adjust phrases that backfire.** If a safety phrase adds fuel to the fire, experiment until one feels genuinely supportive (Nicole).
- **Practice in calm moments.** Short phrases rehearsed during calm periods become accessible when symptoms are intense (Nicole).
- **Build a supportive inner voice.** Use the friend test (Ariel) and a daily self-compassion line (Jon).
- **Swat or deflect unhelpful thoughts** rather than debating them (Junior, Crista, Jon).

### Language guide

- Instead of “Crash” → **“Adjustment period” (AP)**. “Crash” is dramatic and signals danger (Nicole, Jon, Crista). See R-19.
- Instead of “Awful,” “terrible,” “crisis” → **“Challenging,” “temporarily limiting”**. The brain doesn't distinguish joking from truth (Junior).
- Instead of Dramatic metaphors (“my brain is paralyzed”) → **Plain, neutral description**. Language centers connect to the brain's survival center (Crista).
- Instead of “I am sad” → **“I'm experiencing sadness”**. Detachment from experience (Orange Zone, 3.3).
- Instead of “I've gone backwards” → **“This is an adjustment period”**. “The only thing that will make you go backwards is thinking you've gone backwards” (Jon).
- Instead of “I should…” → **“Do I want to? Do I have the capacity?”**. “Should”-driven decisions add pressure (Jon).
- Instead of “I have to get this done” → **“I wonder what I'm capable of”**. Curiosity instead of pressure (Ariel).
- Instead of “When will the symptoms go?” → **“How am I responding to them?”**. Asking when symptoms will go sends danger signals (Jon).
- Instead of (Caregivers) “You'll be fine” → **“I know this is tough”**. False promises backfire when symptoms appear (Junior).

### What we say
- “There is nothing wrong with me.” “It's just my nervous system.” “So what? Whatever.” (Crista's recovery mantras)
- “I'm safe”, repeated, or a longer version such as “I'm safe, I'm happy, I'm healthy, I'm whole, I'm recovering” (Nicole).
- “You did good today, I'm proud of you. This stuff isn't easy.” (Jon)
- “This is just for now. It's not forever.” (Nicole, when asking clients to give something up)

### What we avoid
- Forcing positive affirmations the client doesn't believe.
- Correcting language in a way that feels like criticism; frame it as helping the nervous system hear a different message.
- Arguing with intrusive thoughts line by line.

### Named tools
- **Thought swatting** — Notice the thought, label it (“just a thought”), and don't go on the ride with it. (Junior, Crista)
- **“No thank you” deflection** — Every intrusive thought gets “not right now” or “no thank you,” especially at night. (Jon)
- **Safety words** — One simple phrase for moments when full techniques aren't accessible. (Nicole)
- **Super Fan Voice** — Daily supportive self-talk, using mirrors as cues. (Jon)
- **Friend test** — “How would you talk to a friend you care about in this situation?” (Ariel)

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Feb 2026 · Nicole* — When a client described a flare as a “crash,” Nicole explained why the word matters and replaced it with “adjustment period,” removing the fear attached to the event.
- *Platinum check-in · Apr 2026 · Crista* — A client was repeating affirmations that contradicted how they felt. Crista shifted them to neutral, believable statements the nervous system wouldn't reject.

### Open disagreements
- **Use of “crash.”** Twenty-nine entries show coaches correcting the word, yet it still appears as ordinary vocabulary in about 160 entries across all coaches. Some of this may be the extraction summaries' wording rather than the coaches'. Separately, “AP” is expanded as “activation period” or “activation phase” in 12 entries. See **R-19**.

sourceNote: 489 call entries; most from Jon, Junior, Crista
title: Adjustment Periods, Flare-ups, and Setbacks
summary: Adjustment periods (APs) are how capacity grows.
body:
### Core principle
Adjustment periods (APs) are how capacity grows. A flare after a stretch is expected, and how the client responds, not how intense the symptoms are, determines how the adjustment period plays out.

### What we do

- **Name it.** Call a symptom increase after expansion an adjustment period, and explain that it is the nervous system recalibrating to new stimulus.
- **Pull back, but don't do nothing.** During an AP the goal is to maintain, not expand (Jon, Junior). Keep small anchors of normal life, such as time outside the bedroom or short walks, rather than going into full retreat.
- **Teach the progress cycle.** Expansion, then contraction (the AP), then a recharge phase with waves of feeling better and being pulled back, then emergence at a higher baseline (Jon, Crista). The recharge phase is the most commonly misread.
- **Normalize long adjustment periods.** Eight weeks or more, and even six months or more, fall within normal recovery; longer APs give more repetitions and often precede bigger gains (Crista, Jon).
- **Delay major decisions.** Thinking is clouded during an AP. Hold off on big relationship, career, or travel decisions until the client is through it (Junior); Olga suggests waiting about a week to see stabilization.
- **Prepare higher-capacity clients.** APs can feel more intense after a client has tasted more capacity, because the contrast is bigger (Ariel). Late-stage APs are level-ups, not setbacks (Nicole, Jon).
- **Don't rehearse future APs.** Anticipating the next flare keeps clients living in fear of something that hasn't happened (Junior).

### What we say
- “The only thing that will make you go backwards is thinking you've gone backwards.” (Jon)
- “If you don't respond the same way, it won't play out the same way.” (Jon)
- “You earned it”, for an AP after a long stretch of progress (Jon).
- It's a win-win: if you expand and flare, you got the stimulus you need; if you expand and feel fine, you get to keep expanding (Jon).
- The difference between a crash and an adjustment period is the response, not the intensity (Crista).

### What we avoid
- Treating an AP as regression or evidence the approach has failed.
- Adding a second layer of stress by panicking about the flare (Jon).
- Complete withdrawal, especially for clients who naturally retreat.
- Making several changes at once during an AP (see also M-15).

### Zone adjustments
- **Severe (Red / Orange).** Standard expand-and-contract doesn't work when the floor is already at ground level. Raise the floor through consistency first, before any expansion protocol (Junior).
- **Low to Mid Yellow.** Expand until an AP is triggered; during the AP, pull back but keep minimal activity.
- **High Yellow / Green.** APs are usually shorter and lighter, but can feel emotionally bigger by contrast. Frame them as the final level-ups.

### Common client questions
**Q: How do I know if I'm in an adjustment period?**

If you're expanding and feeling good doing it, you're not; in an AP, expanding is hard and the goal is to maintain (Jon). Junior's check: look at willingness, not symptom level. At 6/10 in an AP you'll say “I'm not feeling it”; out of one, you'll still want to go.

**Q: I've had months of adjustment periods with no progress. Is this working?**

The nervous system sometimes needs more consistency rather than different techniques, and the frustration and hopelessness can themselves be symptoms. Stagnant-looking stretches can still be building the foundation (Nicole).

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Mar 2026 · Jon* — After three and a half months of steady progress, a client was disappointed by a new AP. Jon reframed it as the next level-up that the client had earned by expanding.
- *Platinum check-in · Mar 2026 · Junior* — A client asked whether to keep doing small activities during an AP. Junior drew the line between pulling back and doing nothing, and kept a reduced daily protocol in place.

### Open disagreements
- **When to expand.** Jon's win-win approach (expand until you trigger an AP) and Junior's consistency protocol for severe clients (no expansion on good days until reserves are built) are both taught. They likely apply to different zones, but that isn't written down. See **R-23**.

sourceNote: 852 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Ariel
title: Pacing, Consistency, and Expanding Activity
summary: Capacity grows through consistent, gradual expansion that builds the nervous system's trust.
body:
### Core principle
Capacity grows through consistent, gradual expansion that builds the nervous system's trust. We avoid both extremes: boom-and-bust pushing, and over-resting.

### What we do

- **Increase frequency first, then duration, then intensity** (Jon). Four 5-minute walks are better than two 10-minute walks.
- **Take breaks before symptoms appear.** Junior's biological reset (a voluntary break about every 20 minutes, even when feeling good), Ariel's micro-breaks, and Jon's adapted Pomodoro all build rest in ahead of need.
- **Use flexible ranges, not rigid targets.** “Aim for 4–7 walks per week” or “10–15 minutes” reduces guilt and invites intuition (Ariel).
- **Expand in small steps.** Jon suggests 10–15% increments held for 1–2 weeks; Ariel suggests about 20% when things feel manageable.
- **Decide with manageability.** “What's manageable?” is a repeatable question for big and small decisions (Ariel). Crista's manageability scale targets symptoms around 4–6/10: uncomfortable but manageable.
- **Bank gains on good days.** The urge to catch up on everything creates boom-and-bust; treat new energy like savings rather than spending it all at once (Junior).
- **Balance types of load.** Cognitive, physical, emotional, and social demands all count (Junior, Crista). See R-16.
- **Chunk down valued activities** that feel too demanding: fewer times per week, less volume, with rest days between (Ariel).
- **Separate complex goals into stepping stones,** such as practicing public transport separately from attending a crowded event (Jon).

### What we say
- “Rest is not laziness, it's building trust with your nervous system.” (Jon)
- The nervous system doesn't grade on a curve: pushing through even a little still counts as pushing through (Jon).
- “What have I got left in the tank?” (Jon)
- Physical capacity analogies work for social pacing too: you wouldn't go from 15-minute walks to a 5-mile hike (Crista).

### What we avoid
- Boom-and-bust cycles on good days.
- Pushing through, even “just a little.”
- Over-resting and the belief that recovery requires complete rest (Nicole).
- Waiting for symptoms to reach zero before activity (Junior: “you've waited too long”).
- Rigid daily goals that turn a missed day into failure.

### Named tools
- **Manageability scale** — Target symptoms around 4–6/10: uncomfortable but manageable. Pull back when they become unmanageable. (Crista, Jon, Nicole)
- **Frequency → duration → intensity** — The order for progressing any activity. (Jon)
- **Biological reset / micro-breaks** — Voluntary breaks about every 20 minutes, before symptoms. (Junior, Ariel)
- **Flexible ranges** — Weekly or time ranges instead of exact targets. (Ariel)
- **Savings account** — Build an energy buffer before spending it; used for consistency protocols. (Junior)
- **Labeled timers** — A timer labeled “You'll do this again” counters the urge to squeeze every drop out of rare outings. (Ariel)

### Common client questions
**Q: How do I know when to rest and when to challenge myself?**

You need both. Listen to early signals and take short breaks rather than pushing through; on steadier days, gently challenge. The deciding question is whether symptoms stay manageable and you can respond well (Jon, Ariel).

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · May 2026 · Ariel* — A client felt guilty whenever she missed a daily walk. Ariel replaced the rule with a weekly range, which kept the structure but removed the perfectionist pressure.
- *Platinum check-in · Feb 2026 · Jon* — A client argued they were only pushing through a little. Jon explained that any pushing through reinforces ignoring body signals, regardless of amount.

### Open disagreements
- **When to stop.** Jon's First Signal Stop (stop at the very first, tiniest signal, no exceptions) sits alongside the manageability scale (continue while symptoms are manageable, aiming for 4–6/10), Jon's view that there's “no such thing as too much” if the client responds well afterward, and Junior's rule to never sit with symptoms for more than 15 minutes without some action. See **R-15**.
- **Cognitive versus physical load.** Junior treats them as separate buckets (add cognitive load, reduce physical). Crista treats screen-heavy days as lacking physical balance and adds movement. See **R-16**.

sourceNote: 724 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Responding to Symptoms
summary: “We're not trying to get rid of the symptoms.
body:
### Core principle
“We're not trying to get rid of the symptoms. We're trying to change the way we respond to them.” (Jon) Responding well does not require feeling calm; it means acknowledging the sensation without panic and continuing to live (Junior).

### What we do

- **Teach a neutral response.** “I feel this and I'm okay still” (Junior). “It's okay that this is here. I know it will go, even if it's very strong right now” (Ariel).
- **Take the magnifying glass off.** Reduce body scanning and monitoring, and phase out trackers: heart rate, step counts, and sleep apps (Crista, Jon, Junior, Ariel, Nicole).
- **Give attention somewhere concrete to go.** The feel of hands on a mat, texture and temperature (Junior), or hands resting on the belly (Ariel).
- **Stay gray.** When symptomatic, don't retreat to bed completely; stay on the couch or with family, and don't push through either (Junior). Changing one small element of a symptom routine interrupts the pattern (Crista).
- **Normalize rotating symptoms.** When one symptom resolves and another appears, it's often a sign of progress (Ariel, Crista, Jon).
- **Simplify during brain fog.** The brain is prioritizing threat detection over thinking. Keep things simple (Crista's “cavewoman mode” in upper Yellow) and use frequency over duration for cognitive tasks (Jon).
- **Include emotional symptoms.** Emotional adjustment periods, where the symptoms are mostly emotional, are part of the same process (Crista).
- **Measure over longer windows.** Week-to-week comparisons mislead; two-month comparisons show progress (Jon).

### What we say
- Symptoms are often the last things to leave (Jon).
- “Okay isn't perfect.” You can be okay while having symptoms (Ariel).
- It's 100% okay to have symptoms after something; the question is whether they're manageable and you can respond well (Ariel).

### What we avoid
- Obsessive tracking and pattern-hunting (Jon: looking for patterns puts a magnifying glass on symptoms).
- Forcing strict cause-and-effect links between activity and symptoms; look at manageability over time instead (Ariel).
- Waiting for symptoms to disappear before living.

### Zone adjustments
- **Upper Yellow.** Symptoms may not correlate with activity in the moment, and intense symptoms can give way to normal life within hours. Both are normal (Ariel, Crista).

### Named tools
- **Magnifying glass** — Attention amplifies symptoms; deliberately reduce monitoring. (Crista, Jon)
- **Stay gray** — A middle path between pushing through and full withdrawal during symptoms. (Junior)
- **15-minute rule** — Never sit with symptoms for more than 15 minutes without some small action. (Junior)
- **First Signal Stop** — Stop at the first, tiniest signal during stimulating activities (for example, screens). See R-15. (Jon)
- **Sensory anchoring** — Direct attention to concrete physical sensations during activity. (Junior, Ariel)

### Common client questions
**Q: Should I keep tracking my heart rate to avoid overdoing it?**

Coaches consistently recommend phasing out heart rate, step, and sleep tracking because it feeds hypervigilance (Jon, Crista, Nicole). Where a medical provider has specifically advised monitoring, the client should discuss changes with that provider (see M-15).

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Jun 2026 · Nicole* — A client was anxious about giving up step tracking. Nicole framed it as “just for now,” which lowered the resistance enough for the client to try.
- *Platinum check-in · Feb 2026 · Junior* — Junior described clients who learned to stay present with family during flares instead of going to bed, and who stabilized faster as a result.

### Open disagreements
- **When to stop an activity.** See **R-15** (also in M-04).

### Scope and safety flags
- One Q&A shows a coach assessing whether a client's memory lapses were “residual brain fog rather than cognitive decline” (Platinum, Apr 2026). Distinguishing brain fog from cognitive decline is a medical judgment. See **R-13** and M-15.

sourceNote: 572 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Fear, Anxiety, and Avoidance
summary: The nervous system learns that something is safe through experience, not argument.
body:
### Core principle
The nervous system learns that something is safe through experience, not argument. Clients show safety by doing the activity and by relating well to the symptoms that follow (Jon). At the integration stage, fear is the biggest roadblock (Junior).

### What we do

- **Build evidence through action.** Fear is primal, not logical; clients can't think their way out of it (Junior). See R-17.
- **Label “what ifs” as fears, not facts.** They don't need negotiating. Assume it will be okay, repeat that often, and bring attention back to the present (Jon).
- **Ground in the present moment.** Notice surroundings and remind yourself that in this moment you're safe (Ariel). Stay in the “three-foot world” (Crista, Jon).
- **Approach the original trigger last.** Fear is strongest around the activity linked to the illness's onset; start with similar activities first, such as jogging before cycling (Junior).
- **Watch for safety behaviors.** Look for control behaviors that cascade (one reasonable accommodation leading to many) and for hypervigilance during expansion (Junior).
- **Watch for the comfort-edge loop.** Clients who expand just to mild discomfort and then pull back keep hitting the same wall, like stopping at the first hint of muscle soreness at the gym (Junior).
- **Slow down when symptoms ramp up.** Rushing to safety tells the nervous system there's an emergency (Crista).
- **Reframe “no escape” environments as training.** The escape isn't leaving; it's sitting down, finding a quiet corner, or staying present while symptoms pass (Crista).
- **Normalize health anxiety** and share relevant personal experience where appropriate (Junior).

### What we say
- “Going is the win, not feeling perfect.” (Jon)
- The brain wants to hear not “where's my perfect certainty” but “whatever way it is, we'll still be okay” (Jon).
- “If you don't respond the same way, it won't play out the same way.” (Jon)

### What we avoid
- Reassurance as the main response to fear (Junior, Olga).
- Agreeing with avoidance, such as “maybe you shouldn't walk anymore” (Junior).
- Waiting for perfect circumstances or 100% readiness.
- Rushing, which signals danger.

### Named tools
- **Three-foot world** — Bring attention back to what's within arm's reach right now. (Crista, Jon)
- **Safety bubble assessment** — Map where the client feels safe and what happens when expansion “pops the bubble.” (Junior)
- **Safety behavior plan** — For each danger signal, a specific replacement behavior (stop scanning, allow uncertainty, and so on). (Junior)

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Jun 2026 · Jon* — A client believed a trip required perfect symptom control. Jon redefined success as going, taking breaks as needed, and managing whatever came up.
- *Platinum check-in · May 2026 · Crista* — A client rushed home whenever symptoms ramped up. Crista explained the nervous system's view (“why is this person rushing? Better sound the alarm”) and coached slowing down instead.

### Open disagreements
- **Reassurance and logic.** The Red Zone guide (3.2) tells coaches to offer calm, logic, and reassurance. Call guidance says fear can't be talked away with logic or reassurance, and that hopeless clients want evidence rather than comfort. See **R-17**.

### Scope and safety flags
- A food reintroduction protocol (Platinum, Apr 2026) uses gradual exposure with distraction. Exposure is appropriate for fear-based restriction, but coaches should confirm that true allergies or medically diagnosed intolerances have been ruled out by a provider. See **R-13**.

sourceNote: 261 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Emotional Processing
summary: Emotions need a safe outlet.
body:
### Core principle
Emotions need a safe outlet. Suppressed emotion and constant self-criticism keep danger signals running even when a client is doing everything else right, so we teach clients to feel emotions in manageable doses without adding stories to them.

### What we do

- **Name the emotion and feel it in the body,** without narrative. Crying or other release is fine (Jon).
- **Keep doses manageable.** Short windows of 20 seconds to 2 minutes (Jon), or two breaths if that is the client's current capacity (Olga). If emotional work causes cognitive overwhelm, reduce the duration rather than stopping (Crista).
- **Swat away the stories.** The brain creates analysis and meaning to avoid feeling; redirect back to the sensation (Junior).
- **Validate rather than fix.** “What if this is completely okay to feel this way? What if you don't need to fix it?” (Crista). Frustration is normal; what matters is what you do with it (Nicole).
- **Treat increased emotion as progress.** More crying often means more emotional capacity (Crista). As capacity rises, suppressed emotions may surface during adjustment periods (Jon).
- **Address self-criticism directly.** It often disguises itself as motivation, but it signals danger (Crista).
- **Build emotional stability before physical expansion.** Emotional stability is the foundation physical progress is built on (Crista).

### What we say
- “This is emotional capacity… It's a huge emotional capacity level up.” (Crista)
- Anger is often a protective shell over fear (Junior).

### What we avoid
- Framing emotional processing as a way to get rid of symptoms; it's for wellbeing and healthy nervous system function (Olga).
- Pushing emotions down, or letting them run without limits until they overwhelm.
- Rushing to positive reframes before the emotion has been acknowledged.

### Named tools
- **Scheduled emotional release** — A set daily time (for example, noon) to feel difficult emotions for 1–2 minutes, then actively let go. (Jon)
- **Emotional check-in** — Daily 1–2 minutes asking “do any emotions need to come up?” and then capping it off. (Jon)
- **Emergency notes** — Pre-written phrases and steps on the phone for when activation makes thinking hard. (Jon)

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Jun 2026 · Crista* — A client worried that crying more often meant decline. Crista reframed it as a sign that the nervous system now had capacity to let those emotions through.

### Open disagreements
- **Scheduled versus real-time processing.** Jon teaches time-capped, scheduled releases. Junior teaches that most processing should happen in real time as emotions arise, and Crista emphasizes letting clients grieve without fixing. These may suit different clients, but there's no shared guidance on when to use which. See **R-20**.

sourceNote: 994 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Mindset: Hope, Patience, and Progress
summary: Mindset keeps the boat afloat (Part 2.6).
body:
### Core principle
Mindset keeps the boat afloat (Part 2.6). We build hope on evidence, help clients be patient with their own timeline, and teach acceptance that is surrender to the body's pace, not giving up.

### What we do

- **Make progress visible.** Draw concrete then-and-now comparisons (Junior), show movement on the nervous system assessment triangle (Jon), and look back at where the client started (Crista).
- **Teach acceptance of current capacity.** Acceptance is the biggest overrider of frustration (Jon); it isn't giving up.
- **Take guilt off the table.** The client didn't ask for this condition, and guilt itself sends danger signals (Jon).
- **Treat demotivation as a symptom.** Action doesn't require motivation (Jon).
- **Normalize the pendulum.** Swings between hope and despair are part of the process (Junior), and stress comes in seasons (Junior).
- **Invite full commitment.** Clients who hold back to protect themselves from disappointment reduce their chances; ask what they have to lose by committing fully (Jon).
- **Encourage growing through, not just going through,** by using illness as a chance to examine patterns (Junior).
- **Recognize the stages.** Clients move from symptom-focused to recovery-focused to life-focused (Ariel). Around any activity there are three moments: anticipatory anxiety, mindset during, and processing afterward (Jon).

### What we say
- “I have yet to hop on a call where someone's like, I wish recovery would slow down. We all feel that way.” (Crista)
- “You never know how far you are from gold.” (Jon)
- There's a difference between suffering and suffering with purpose: each AP is another layer being unpeeled (Jon).

### What we avoid
- Forced positivity or skipping validation.
- Timeline pressure, such as “I should be further along at five months” (Crista).
- Comparison with other clients; comparative thoughts are a form of hypervigilance (Ariel).

### Common client questions
**Q: How do I handle guilt around my condition, as if I'm to blame?**

Recognize you didn't ask for this and it's not your fault. Guilt makes the nervous system feel under threat, and it usually comes from feeling you should be doing more (Jon).

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Mar 2026 · Junior* — Junior listed a client's concrete changes since joining (living independently, a relationship, considering work) to counter the feeling that nothing had improved.

sourceNote: 83 call entries; most from Jon, Junior, Crista
title: Personality Patterns: Perfectionism, People-Pleasing, All-or-Nothing
summary: Black-and-white patterns (pushing hard when well, retreating in fear when unwell) keep the nervous system dysregulated.
body:
### Core principle
Black-and-white patterns (pushing hard when well, retreating in fear when unwell) keep the nervous system dysregulated. Recovery happens in the gray area. This builds on Part 2.2: traits don't cause the illness, but some patterns can keep it going.

### What we do

- **Name the swing and aim for the middle.** Too much enthusiasm then withdrawal, too much structure then chaos: recovery lives between the extremes (Jon).
- **Channel drive instead of fighting it.** Be the best at responding well, the best at restraint (Jon); redirect competitive energy toward recovery goals (Crista).
- **Match the strategy to the person.** Pushers need permission to rest; fear-based clients need gentle challenge. Don't apply one person's strategy to another (Junior).
- **Teach gray-area boundaries** that are kind and self-protective, instead of no boundaries or brick walls (Crista).
- **Separate self-worth from productivity.** Worth comes from self-compassion, not external validation (Junior).
- **Ask “is this a moment or a lifestyle?”** Intense effort with an end date is different from grinding as a default identity (Junior).
- **Use “What would I have done before?”** to spot old patterns and choose differently (Junior).
- **Use flexible ranges** to take perfectionist pressure out of plans (Ariel, M-04).

### What we say
- New thought patterns are like cutting a dirt track through brambles; keep going and it becomes a path (Jon).
- People-pleasing is a nervous system seeking safety and support; the key is awareness without judgment (Crista).

### What we avoid
- Shaming clients for their traits.
- Encouraging clients to do recovery “exactly right,” which becomes another form of perfectionism (Junior).

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Feb 2026 · Jon* — A Type A client wanted to push his way to recovery. Jon asked him to channel the same drive into becoming the best at responding to symptoms.

### Open disagreements
- **How we talk about traits.** Part 2.2 says certain personality traits may keep illness going; Crista tells clients that people-pleasing is “not true personality traits” but a nervous system seeking safety. Both avoid blame, but the framing should be consistent. See **R-26**.

sourceNote: 277 call entries; most from Jon, Junior, Crista
title: Exercise and Movement
summary: Exercise is reintroduced like any other expansion: frequency first, in small doses, and in ways that stop the brain from tagging movement as dangerous.
body:
### Core principle
Exercise is reintroduced like any other expansion: frequency first, in small doses, and in ways that stop the brain from tagging movement as dangerous.

### What we do

- **Start smaller than feels necessary.** Five minutes of gentle stretching 2–3 times a week, building to daily, before adding duration (Jon). “Exercise snacking” uses sessions as short as 30–40 seconds (Jon).
- **Begin with simple movements,** such as calf raises, hip raises, and shoulder movements, before squats and push-ups (Jon); or two supported mini squats and two wall push-ups daily (Crista).
- **Don't lie down to analyze afterward.** Move straight into a different activity, even five minutes of cognitive work, so the brain doesn't isolate the exercise as a threat (Jon).
- **Split longer walks** into two shorter sessions (Nicole).
- **Use lingering soreness as the signal.** Soreness that lasts several days means more recovery time is needed (Crista).
- **Don't let one workout take the blame** for an AP when the stress bucket was already full (Crista, M-01).
- **Choose valued activities.** Clients don't need to force walks they don't value if another activity suits them better (Ariel).
- **Save the original trigger activity for later** (Junior, M-06).

### What we avoid
- Jumping to demanding exercise because it seems “healthy.”
- Retreating to rest immediately after every session.
- Treating a single hard session as proof that exercise is dangerous.

### Zone adjustments
- **Severe.** Where activities last seconds, increase how often before how long (Jon).
- **Late recovery.** Clients who handle daily life (5,000–7,500 steps, household tasks) still rebuild specific capacities, such as hills, gradually (Crista).

### Named tools
- **Exercise snacking** — Very brief, frequent movement sessions. (Jon)
- **Activity sandwiching** — Follow physical activity immediately with a different kind of activity. (Jon)

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Apr 2026 · Jon* — For a late-stage client returning to strength work, Jon started with a short daily routine of simple stretches rather than a full workout.

sourceNote: 95 call entries; most from Jon, Junior, Crista
title: Sleep and Rest
summary: Sleep improves when it stops being a performance with a score.
body:
### Core principle
Sleep improves when it stops being a performance with a score. We reduce monitoring and pressure around sleep, and treat improved sleep as a meaningful sign of regulation.

### What we do

- **Change the goal from sleep to rest.** Ask “What can I do that's restful?”; sometimes wired energy needs to be spent gently first (Ariel).
- **Deflect night-time thoughts** with “not right now” or “no thank you” and a simple breath count (Jon).
- **Stop sleep tracking.** Turn clocks around, don't check the time, and remove sleep apps (Crista).
- **Don't forecast the day from hours slept.** “I have just enough energy to get started. Let's see how the day goes” (Crista).
- **Avoid building strong links** between sleep and specific symptoms (Jon).
- **Keep naps under an hour;** guided relaxation such as Yoga Nidra can help (Junior).
- **Create a buffer from screens,** with 1–2 hours before bed and no phone in the bedroom (Jon).
- **Normalize flips and shifts.** Reversed sleep schedules are common and adjustable; needing a little more sleep during expansion isn't regression (Crista, Jon).

### What we avoid
- Treating one bad night as a ruined day.
- Intensive sleep monitoring.
- Eliminating naps entirely before improving how mornings go (Crista).

### From the calls
- *Caregiver call · Dec 2025 · Junior* — A caregiver said their loved one wasn't improving. Junior pointed out that going from almost no sleep to hours every night was major progress, even though other symptoms felt worse.

### Scope and safety flags
- One Q&A (Platinum, Mar 2026) instructs a client to delay taking prescribed sleep medication by two hours each night. Changes to medication timing belong with the prescriber. See **R-13** and M-15.

sourceNote: 129 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Work, Career, and Study
summary: Returning to work or study is an expansion like any other: phased, protected by boundaries, and expected to bring an adjustment period.
body:
### Core principle
Returning to work or study is an expansion like any other: phased, protected by boundaries, and expected to bring an adjustment period. Being ready enough matters more than being perfectly ready.

### What we do

- **Use three guardrails for big decisions:** Do I want to (not should I)? Do I have the capacity? How will I protect myself? (Jon)
- **Phase the return.** Start with part-time work or volunteering, even one afternoon a week, before full-time (Jon). Low-pressure stepping stones are fine (Integration, Dec 2025).
- **Expect an adjustment period on return.** It shows the client can handle new demands even with symptoms (Jon).
- **Use curiosity language:** “I wonder what I'm capable of” instead of “I have to get this done” (Ariel).
- **Build cognitive stamina deliberately,** for example five pages of reading a day or self-paced courses (Jon), with micro-breaks every 20 minutes (Ariel).
- **Prioritize when capacity is full.** Focus on the top two or three values (Crista). If work is non-negotiable, create space elsewhere (Crista).
- **Set workplace limits.** Most requests aren't emergencies; with Crista's cat analogy, a client asks “which cat would you like me to drop?”
- **Expect a decompression phase** after deadlines; lower capacity afterward isn't regression (Jon).
- **Treat a demanding career as a pacing challenge** before assuming it must be abandoned (Ariel).

### What we say
- “We're never 100% ready… But if you're even just like 60% ready, that's kind of enough.” (Jon)
- Take the next forward step in order to figure things out, rather than figuring everything out first (Crista).

### What we avoid
- Going straight back to full-time work.
- “Should”-driven decisions. People-pleasers should do less than they think they can (Jon).

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Apr 2026 · Jon* — A client feared a September return to work would bring back past symptoms. Jon agreed an adjustment period was likely and reframed it as a normal recalibration the client now knew how to respond to.

sourceNote: 399 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Relationships, Social Life, and Travel
summary: Social life and travel are graded exposures.
body:
### Core principle
Social life and travel are graded exposures. We help clients take part in a modified way, set boundaries early and kindly, and expect normal adjustment when returning home.

### What we do

- **Treat social events as experiments,** not commitments (Crista).
- **Start with safe, predictable people** before adding “wild cards” (Crista).
- **Set boundaries before they're needed,** for example “I'll need short breaks every 25 minutes” (Jon).
- **Start with one relationship and one boundary.** Clients can lean on the coach: “my coach is recommending…” (Crista).
- **Use “two things can be true”:** people can mean well and still be hurtful (Junior).
- **Plan modified participation** instead of all-or-nothing: “I'll do as much as I can, and I'll be OK with however much that is” (Jon).
- **Build recovery time between trips,** and expect symptoms on returning home as the nervous system readjusts (Junior, Ariel).
- **Offer to include a confused family member** in a session (Crista).
- **Support within capacity.** Choosing emotional availability over physical rescue is growth, not selfishness (Ariel).

### What we avoid
- All-or-nothing trip decisions.
- Rushing during travel (arrive early, allow extra time).
- Boundaries that are either absent or brick walls (M-09).

### Named tools
- **Labeled timers** — Timers for social time labeled “You'll have opportunity again.” (Ariel)
- **Headphones cue** — Wearing earbuds as a visual signal discourages unwanted conversations. (Ariel)
- **Graded participation** — Take part in part of an event or trip rather than all or none. (Jon)

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · May 2026 · Crista* — A client dreaded hosting guests during an adjustment period. Crista framed the visit as an experiment rather than a commitment.

sourceNote: 117 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Ariel
title: Later-Stage Recovery and Life After
summary: Late recovery is long and layered.
body:
### Core principle
Late recovery is long and layered. The focus shifts from recovery to life, and lasting recovery depends on emotional and mindset stability, not just physical capacity.

### What we do

- **Expect a long final stage.** Clients can feel functionally recovered but still have symptoms and occasional APs, potentially for years (Jon). Glimpses of full wellness followed by symptoms are normal (Crista).
- **Recognize recovery in layers.** Clients may think they're recovered, then meet a “final exam” that shows there's more to consolidate (Crista).
- **Change the daily question** from “What do I need to do for my recovery today?” to “What do I need to do today?” (Jon).
- **Welcome outgrowing recovery spaces.** Losing interest in recovery content is a healthy sign (Junior, Ariel).
- **Move from rules to intuition.** Structured plans are gradually overridden by the client's own judgment (Junior). See R-21.
- **Assess readiness by stretch capacity.** Ask “If there were an emergency, could you walk 40 minutes?” rather than relying on conservative daily choices (Ariel).
- **Mark the normal-tired milestone.** Tiredness that offers choices, rather than a sudden shutdown, is significant progress (Crista).
- **Protect against relapse** by making sure emotional and mindset stability are in place, not just physical capacity (Junior).
- **Create a recovery file** of wins, transcripts, and tools the client can return to if needed (Jon).

### What we avoid
- Treating late-stage APs as evidence recovery isn't real.
- Keeping clients in recovery-focused routines they have outgrown.

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Mar 2026 · Junior* — A client was frightened by stories of recovered people relapsing. Junior explained that those relapses usually followed physical recovery without emotional and mindset stability, which the client was actively building.

### Open disagreements
- **Transparent versus covert techniques.** Junior's “Secret Intuition Building” gives a client a fixed plan with the hidden intention that they'll outgrow it. See **R-21**.

*This module offers material for the Green Zone gaps in 3.5 (R-07).*

sourceNote: 130 call entries; most from Junior, Crista, Ariel
title: Medical Care, Medication, and Other Treatments
summary: Coaches support how clients relate to medical care.
body:
### Core principle
Coaches support how clients relate to medical care. Decisions about diagnosis, medication, supplements, and treatment belong to clients and their medical providers. (The second sentence is proposed; see the recommended standard below.)

### What we do

- **Frame medication by intention.** Taken as support to participate in life, medication sends a safety message, like an ice pack for an injury. Taken from fear, it reinforces danger (Ariel).
- **Help clients notice over-treatment.** Clients can accumulate protocols, supplements, and appointments that keep the nervous system activated. Help them reflect on whether each one provides relief or adds stress, while the decisions stay with them and their providers (Junior).
- **Watch for too many simultaneous approaches.** Several therapies and programs at once can drain the energy needed for recovery (Nicole).
- **Avoid the convenience trap.** Clients don't need to pause all recovery work while dealing with something else; make gentle progress in parallel (Junior).
- **Prepare clients for medical appointments.** Speak honestly and simply; the goal is taking care of yourself, not getting validation (Ariel).
- **Expect temporary symptom changes around prescribed changes,** and help clients respond calmly rather than panic (Crista, Ariel).

### What we say
- “The coach cannot provide medical recommendations”: boundary language already used on a Platinum call (Junior, Mar 2026).

### What we avoid
- See the scope flags and recommended standard below.

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Apr 2026 · Ariel* — A client asked whether ibuprofen was “fixing” symptoms and setting recovery back. Ariel focused on intention (support to participate in life versus fear) without advising on the medication itself.

### Scope and safety flags
- Coaches gave specific tapering guidance for SSRIs, including a rate (“1mg at a time”) (Platinum, Jun 2026).
- A coach instructed a client to delay prescribed sleep medication by two hours each night (Platinum, Mar 2026).
- Symptoms during a cortisone taper were reframed as nervous system adjustment (Platinum, Mar 2026). Steroid tapers can cause medically significant withdrawal effects.
- A client with health anxiety was told “You don't need to [take medication or supplements] because there's nothing to cure, you're completely fine” (Platinum, Jun 2026).
- A client was coached to continue their day through symptoms from food or medication (Platinum, May 2026), without distinguishing a possible adverse reaction.
- A program insight says continued medication use “should be questioned” if benefit isn't clear (Platinum, Apr 2026).
- Related: brain fog versus cognitive decline (M-05), food reintroduction (M-06), and advice not to change supplements during adjustment periods (Crista, Mar 2026). That last one is reasonable caution, but it is still medical direction.

### Recommended standard (proposed, not yet adopted)
1. Coaches do not advise on starting, stopping, tapering, dosing, or timing medications or supplements. We encourage clients to discuss any change with their prescriber, and we can help them manage the nervous system side of a change their provider has agreed.
2. Coaches do not judge whether a symptom is or isn't medical. New, severe, or changing symptoms are a reason to see a medical provider, and we support clients in doing that calmly.
3. Exposure work involving food, or exercise with a diagnosed condition, proceeds only where a provider has ruled out risks such as true allergy.
4. Where a provider has prescribed monitoring (for example, heart rate), coaches don't tell clients to stop it; they encourage a conversation with the provider.

sourceNote: 352 call entries; most from Junior, Jon, Crista
title: Coaching Presence and Technique
summary: How we coach matters as much as what we teach.
body:
### Core principle
How we coach matters as much as what we teach. We normalize quickly and specifically, validate before redirecting, and fit our explanations to the client in front of us.

### What we do

- **Normalize fast and specifically.** “Very common. Very, very common”, followed where appropriate by the coach's own similar experience (Nicole). When clients think their history makes them unrecoverable, share specific examples of recovery from similar backgrounds (Crista).
- **Validate before redirecting.** Clients who feel invalidated won't be open to what comes next (Crista, Junior).
- **Fit analogies to how the client thinks.** A savings account suits logical clients (Junior); physical analogies help with social pacing (Crista).
- **Name and celebrate transformation.** “This is what lasting recovery looks like”, tied to specific examples (Crista).
- **Hold big answers until the client can hear them.** “I wouldn't have answered your question if you were still in it” (Junior, about a question raised during an AP).
- **Strip it back when clients are overwhelmed.** One phrase instead of a protocol: “This is just my nervous system. There's nothing wrong with me” (Jon).
- **For bedbound clients, follow the client's own stop signals** and respect them immediately (Ariel).
- **Name patterns kindly and directly,** for example inconsistency or giving up before results show (Jon).
- **Use the community.** Peer support during hard periods offers something coaching can't (Crista).
- **Don't copy one client's plan onto another** (Junior, M-09).

### What we avoid
- Leading with fixes before the client feels heard.
- Delivering complex, multi-step protocols to a dysregulated client.
- Generic encouragement where a specific example would land better.

### From the calls
- *Platinum check-in · Mar 2026 · Nicole* — A client was embarrassed by her limitations. Nicole immediately named how common this was and shared her own experience of tying her worth to what she could do.

### Open disagreements
- **Reassurance** (see **R-17**) and **transparency of techniques** (see **R-21**) both affect coaching presence.

*For Red Zone clients, trust-building comes first (3.2).*

sourceNote: 349 call entries; most from Junior, Olga, Chelsea
title: Supporting Caregivers
summary: Caregivers help most by bringing calm presence and accurate, neutral language, supporting gradual expansion without enforcing avoidance, and protectin.
body:
### Core principle
Caregivers help most by bringing calm presence and accurate, neutral language, supporting gradual expansion without enforcing avoidance, and protecting their own wellbeing. (Caregiver calls refer to the client as the “Thriver.”)

### What we do

**Understanding the condition**

- **Anger is often fear in disguise,** for example about noise making things worse (Junior).
- **Constant symptoms suggest constant danger signals** the person may not be aware of, such as monitoring or worry (Junior).
- **The nervous system pays attention to how things end.** A bad ending colors the whole experience (Junior).
- **Delayed flares follow the two-tank pattern:** adrenaline masks fatigue in the moment (Junior, M-01).
- **Early progress is stability, not capacity:** better sleep, longer calm periods, less anger (Junior).

**Communicating**

- **Use neutral, accurate language** rather than reassuring promises (Junior).
- **Offer one brief acknowledgment** (“I know this is tough”), then nonverbal comfort and your own calm presence (Junior).
- **Validate the fear exists** while staying steady: “I know you're scared. I get it. And I'm going to be here” (Olga).
- **Wait for emotions to settle** before discussing patterns; logic doesn't reach someone in a danger response (Junior, Olga).

**Practical support**

- **End activities while the person still feels relatively okay,** so experiences end well (Junior).
- **Don't wait for symptoms to reach zero** before trying again (Junior, race car analogy).
- **Gently reintroduce feared activities** with your presence; avoidance deepens fear (Junior).
- **Don't enforce complete silence** for sound sensitivity, as it confirms that sound is dangerous (Junior). See R-22.
- **Don't rush preparation time;** arrive early when traveling (Junior).
- **Don't let the person isolate completely** during long adjustment periods (Junior).

**Boundaries**

- **Your part is to offer accurate information and reframes;** whether they integrate them is theirs (Junior).
- **Respect a request to be alone** during an adjustment period (Junior).
- **Advocating doesn't mean hiding information** or making decisions for them (Caregiver call, Jan 2026).
- **Time apart can build independence** (Junior).
- **Know the limits of lay caregiving.** When care needs exceed what an untrained caregiver can provide, or rumination persists despite support, professional help is appropriate (Junior).

**Caregiver wellbeing**

- **Breaks are necessary, not abandonment;** a weekend away with trusted cover is self-care (Junior).
- **Share the load** across more than one caregiver where possible (Olga).
- **Process your own emotions** and regulate yourself first; your face and body language communicate your state (Olga).

### What we avoid
- Saying “you did too much,” “get ready for the eventual crash,” or “everything will be okay” without evidence (Junior).
- Long lists of affirmations or repeated reassurance during distress (Junior).
- Working together to constantly fix symptoms (Olga).
- Showing disappointment when part of a plan is missed (Olga).
- Arguing with high emotion, or entertaining endless rumination loops (Olga, Junior).
- Telling someone their psychological roadblock when they lack the capacity to hear it (Junior).

### Common client questions
**Q: How do I communicate hope when my loved one doesn't believe reassurance?**

Don't lead with hope or vague reassurance. Use accuracy: “Your system is overwhelmed and protecting you right now. This is predictable. We're not looking for huge progress, just one small sign that your capacity hasn't disappeared.” Hope builds through glimmers and pattern recognition (Junior).

**Q: My child has anticipatory anxiety and feels awful hours after activities, and now refuses to go. What do I do?**

Use neutral rather than reassuring language, avoid promising they'll feel fine, and help make activities end while they still feel okay (Junior).

### From the calls
- *Caregiver call · Dec 2025 · Olga* — A caregiver's instinct was to tell their loved one “it's not COVID” during a fear spike. Olga shifted them to validating the fear and staying calmly present.

### Open disagreements
- **Check-ins.** Caregivers were told to continuously check in (“How do you feel right now? Good or not so good?”) (Feb 2026), and also to avoid repeatedly asking how their loved one is feeling (Apr 2024, Mar 2026). See **R-18**.
- **Covert exercises.** Caregivers were advised not to tell a fearful loved one that an activity is an “exercise” (Apr 2026). See **R-21**.
- **Exposure in severe cases.** Gentle sound exposure over a loved one's anger conflicts with the Red Zone emphasis on deep rest and sensitivity to light and sound (3.2). See **R-22**.

### Scope and safety flags
- Caregivers were advised not to reason with a loved one saying “I don't want to be here anymore”, but to wait until they're calm and then work on the black-and-white thinking (May 2026). That statement can signal suicidal thoughts and needs a safety response first. See M-18 and **R-14**.
- Caregiver calls are a private space, and recordings aren't shared with Thrivers (Jan 2026). When this content moves to the wiki, make sure caregiver material isn't visible to clients.
